levels.title: Remember the Last Word
levels.story: Wren reads a long note aloud and Kit has to answer a question about its first line. By the end, the beginning is hazy. "You read a word at a time and carried a summary," says Wren. "A program can do that too. The trouble is how long the summary lasts."

everyday.scene: When you read a sentence, you do not look at all the words at once. You read one at a time and keep a feel for what came before.
everyday.question: How could a program read a sentence one word at a time and still remember the start?
everyday.answer: It keeps a running summary, called a hidden state, and updates it with each new word. This is the idea behind a recurrent neural network.

lessons.title: A running summary
text: A recurrent neural network, or RNN, reads a sequence one step at a time. It keeps a hidden state, a form of memory, updated at each step from the new word and the old state.
The same learned step is used at every position, so the network can read a sentence of any length. That repeating is where the name recurrent comes from.

terms.meaning: The network's running summary of what it has read so far.
One word, or one position, in the sequence.

references.title: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Recurrent Neural Networks

lessons.title: Memory that fades
text: Here is a toy version. At each step, the new memory is half the old memory plus the new word's signal. A signal of 1 on the first word becomes 1, then 0.5, 0.25, 0.125 and 0.0625 as four zeros follow.

text.text: Real networks learn their own numbers, but a plain RNN has a similar problem. Traditional RNNs suffer from the vanishing gradient problem, which limits their ability to learn long-range dependencies, so linking words far apart is hard.

lessons.title: Remembering longer
text: In 'the keys that Wren left on the old table by the window were lost', the verb 'were' depends on 'keys', which is 11 words earlier. A plain RNN may have lost the clue by then.

The long short-term memory network, or LSTM, from 1997, adds gates that decide what to keep and what to forget. It was designed to ease the vanishing gradient problem. It still reads one word at a time.

deeper.title: Reading in order
text: Because an RNN must finish one word before starting the next, it cannot read all the words at once, which makes training slower on long texts.

activities.prompt: In the toy memory, word 1 sets the memory to 1. Word 2 carries 0. What is the memory after word 2?
hints: Halve the old memory and add the new signal.

activities.explain: Each step halves the memory, so the first word's signal shrinks to almost nothing by word 5.

steps.say: A toy memory reads five words. After each word its memory number becomes half the old number plus the new word's signal. Word 1 carries a signal of 1 and words 2 to 5 carry 0. Each box will show the memory after that word.
After word 1, the memory is 0.5 x 0 + 1 = 1. The first word is fully remembered.
After word 2, the memory is 0.5 x 1 + 0 = 0.5. Half of the first word's signal has faded.

predict.prompt: The memory is 1 and word 2 carries 0. What is the memory after word 2?
hints: Halve the old memory, then add the new signal.

steps.say: After word 3, the memory is 0.25. Each step halves it again.

predict.prompt: The memory is 0.5 and word 3 carries 0. What is it after word 3?

steps.say: By word 5 the memory is 0.0625. The first word's signal has nearly vanished, and longer sentences would shrink it further. That fading is why plain recurrent networks struggle to link words that are far apart.

activities.explain: After word 2 it is 0.5, then 0.25, 0.125 and 0.0625.

fieldNotes.title: Recurrent networks
fieldNotes.text: An RNN's recurrent unit keeps a hidden state, a form of memory, which is updated at each step from the current input and the previous hidden state.

fieldNotes.title: LSTMs
fieldNotes.text: Long short-term memory networks were published in 1997 and are a type of RNN aimed at easing the vanishing gradient problem.

fieldNotes.title: Text from RNNs
fieldNotes.text: RNNs have been trained to write text one character at a time, learning to copy the style of the text they were given.

source.title: The Unreasonable Effectiveness of Recurrent Neural Networks

summary: You saw a recurrent network read one word at a time with a hidden state, watched a toy memory fade over a few steps, and learned why LSTMs add gates.
Wren sets down the long note. "You kept the start for a while. A gate might have kept it longer."

mistake.title: Thinking memory lasts forever
mistake.text: A hidden state is a small summary updated at every step. Old information fades unless the network has a way, like gates, to hold on to it.
